quests.instruction: Say “Nice to meet you” quickly. What happens where “meet” and “you” join?
options: The /t/ is left out entirely, so it sounds like “mee-you” with a clear “y”
The /t/ moves onto “you”, giving “mee-tyou” with both sounds kept
The /t/ and /j/ blend into a new /tʃ/ sound: “mee-choo”
The /j/ is left out, so it sounds like “meet-oo” with a clear /t/ released
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ and /j/ blend into a new /tʃ/ sound: “mee-choo”
quests.hint: Say “meet you” slowly, then at conversation speed. Notice whether you still hear a separate /t/ and a separate “y” sound.
quests.explanation: At normal speed, the tongue does not have time to make a /t/ and then a /j/ separately. The two sounds merge into one new sound, /tʃ/, the “ch” of “church”: “mee-choo”. This is called coalescence. It explains why you may know both words yet fail to recognise them when they run together.
quests.phoneticRule: In coalescence, two adjacent sounds merge into a single new sound that combines features of both: /t/ + /j/ commonly becomes /tʃ/.

quests.instruction: In “Great to meet you all”, which statement best describes what coalescence is?
options: Two neighbouring sounds merge into one new sound that blends features of both
One sound disappears completely, leaving the other unchanged
One sound changes place to match the next sound but stays separate
A vowel is inserted between two sounds to keep them apart
quests.correctAnswer: Two neighbouring sounds merge into one new sound that blends features of both
quests.hint: Compare what you learned about elision, assimilation and linking. Which of them creates a third sound?
quests.explanation: In elision a sound is lost, in assimilation one sound changes to resemble its neighbour but is still there, and in linking a sound moves to the next word unchanged. Coalescence is different: the two sounds disappear into one new sound. In “meet you”, /t/ and /j/ become /tʃ/.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescence differs from elision, assimilation and linking because the output is a single new segment that replaces two input segments.

quests.instruction: Apply the idea to “let you” in “I’ll let you go”. Which spoken form fits?
options: “let-you”: both sounds are fully pronounced with a pause between them
“le-doo”: the /t/ becomes a /d/ before the /j/
“lesh-oo”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into a /ʃ/ sound
“le-choo”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
quests.correctAnswer: “le-choo”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
quests.hint: The word “let” ends in /t/ and the next word starts with /j/. Recall which sound the pair blended into in the previous question.
quests.explanation: The same /t/ + /j/ pair is present, so you predict the same result: /tʃ/, giving “le-choo”. The pattern depends on the sounds, not on the particular words. Once you know the rule, you can predict it for any /t/ followed by “you”.
quests.phoneticRule: The result of coalescence is predictable from the input sounds, so /t/ + /j/ gives /tʃ/ in any word pair where a /t/ meets /j/.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “don’t you” fits “Don’t you think so?”
options: “dohnt-you”: both sounds are pronounced separately with a pause
“dohn-choo”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
“dohn-doo”: the /t/ becomes a /d/
“dohn-oo”: the /t/ and /j/ are both dropped
quests.correctAnswer: “dohn-choo”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
quests.hint: Say “don’t you” as you would in a friendly question, quickly. Listen for what happens after the /n/.
quests.explanation: “Don’t” ends in /t/ and “you” begins with /j/, so the pair blends into /tʃ/: “dohn-choo”. Tag-like questions such as this are very common, so the blend is one of the sounds you hear most often. It sounds like a different word until you know the pattern.
quests.phoneticRule: Negative contractions ending in /t/ blend with a following “you”: /t/ + /j/ becomes /tʃ/, as in “don’t you” and “won’t you”.

quests.instruction: In “Say what you mean”, which sound do the /t/ of “what” and the /j/ of “you” become?
options: /dʒ/: the “j” sound as in “jam”
/ʃ/: the “sh” sound as in “shoe”
/tʃ/: the “ch” sound
/t/: the /j/ simply disappears
quests.correctAnswer: /tʃ/: the “ch” sound
quests.hint: Compare the first sound of “church” with the first sound of “shoe”, and decide which one begins with a stop.
quests.explanation: The /t/ is a voiceless stop and the /j/ is a smooth glide. When they merge, the result keeps the stop quality of the /t/ and the palatal place of the /j/, so you hear /tʃ/: “wot-chu mean”. The weak “you” (/jə/) makes the blend even more likely.
quests.phoneticRule: The blend /tʃ/ is an affricate: it keeps the stop closure of /t/ and the palatal release of /j/, which is why it sounds like “ch”.

quests.instruction: Apply the pattern to “won’t you” in “Won’t you join us?” Which spoken form fits?
options: “wohn-choo”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
“wohnt-you”: both sounds are pronounced separately
“wohn-shoo”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /ʃ/ instead
“wohn-joo”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/ instead
quests.correctAnswer: “wohn-choo”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
quests.hint: The first word ends in /t/, exactly as in the last two questions. Predict the result before you check the options.
quests.explanation: “Won’t” ends in /t/ and “you” begins with /j/, so the result is /tʃ/: “wohn-choo”. An invitation like this is more natural with the blend than with a clearly separated “wont you”. Hearing the blend helps you recognise the invitation in fast speech.
quests.phoneticRule: The /t/ + /j/ blend applies to invitations and offers in the same way as to questions and statements.

quests.instruction: What happens where “would” and “you” meet in “Would you like some tea?”
options: The /d/ is left out, so it sounds like “wou-you”
The /d/ becomes a /t/, so it sounds like “wou-choo”
The two sounds stay separate with a short stop between them
The /d/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/, so it sounds like “wou-ja”
quests.correctAnswer: The /d/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/, so it sounds like “wou-ja”
quests.hint: Say “would you” quickly and listen to the sound between the vowels of the two words.
quests.explanation: “Would” ends in /d/ and “you” begins with /j/. The pair blends into /dʒ/, the “j” of “judge”: “wou-ja”. The /d/ is voiced, so the result is also voiced; this is why it is /dʒ/ and not /tʃ/. Polite offers such as this one use the blend constantly.
quests.phoneticRule: A voiced /d/ + /j/ gives the voiced affricate /dʒ/, just as voiceless /t/ + /j/ gives /tʃ/: the voicing of the first sound is kept.

quests.instruction: Why does “told you” sound like “tol-joo” in “Told you it would rain”?
options: The /l/ of “told” blends with the /j/ to form /dʒ/
The word “told” is replaced by the word “toll” in fast speech here
The /j/ is replaced by a /d/ to match “told”
The /d/ of “told” blends with the /j/ of “you” to form /dʒ/
quests.correctAnswer: The /d/ of “told” blends with the /j/ of “you” to form /dʒ/
quests.hint: Look at the last sound of “told” and the first sound of “you”. Which pair can blend?
quests.explanation: “Told” ends in the cluster /ld/, and the last sound, /d/, meets the /j/ of “you”. They blend into /dʒ/: “tol-joo”. The /l/ is not involved, so it stays. Pairs like “told you” show that the pattern works after consonant clusters too.
quests.phoneticRule: Only the final /d/ of a cluster enters the blend with /j/; the sounds before it remain unchanged.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “did you” fits “Did you eat lunch?”
options: “did-you”: both words are strong with a clear /j/
“di-ja”: the /d/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/, and “you” is a weak /jə/
“di-cha”: the /d/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
“dih-a”: the /d/ and /j/ are dropped
quests.correctAnswer: “di-ja”: the /d/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/, and “you” is a weak /jə/
quests.hint: This is probably the most common blend in English. Say the question the way a friend would.
quests.explanation: “Did you” is spoken as “di-ja” far more often than as two separate words. The /d/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/, and “you” is reduced to /jə/. If you have ever heard “didja” and wondered what it meant, this is where it comes from.
quests.phoneticRule: The pair “did you” combines blending (/d/ + /j/ → /dʒ/) with weak-form reduction of “you” to /jə/.

quests.instruction: Predict what happens where “miss” and “you” meet in “Lee will miss you”.
options: “mi-shoo”: the /s/ and /j/ blend into /ʃ/
“mi-zhoo”: they blend into /ʒ/
“mi-choo”: they blend into /tʃ/
“miss-you”: nothing happens, because /s/ cannot blend with /j/
quests.correctAnswer: “mi-shoo”: the /s/ and /j/ blend into /ʃ/
quests.hint: The /s/ is voiceless and the /j/ is a glide. Predict a result that is also voiceless, and made further back.
quests.explanation: A voiceless /s/ meets a /j/, so the blend is the voiceless “sh” sound, /ʃ/: “mi-shoo”. The tongue moves back towards the position of /j/, and the hiss becomes a “sh”. The rule keeps the voicing of the first sound, as in the earlier levels.
quests.phoneticRule: Voiceless /s/ + /j/ gives voiceless /ʃ/, so the voicing of the first sound is preserved in the blend.

quests.instruction: Why does “this year” often sound like “thi-shear” in “Prices rise this year”?
options: The /s/ is replaced by /ʃ/ only because “year” is spelled with a letter “y”
The /s/ and /j/ blend into /ʃ/, as the tongue moves back for the /j/
The /j/ moves onto “this”, giving “thisy ear”
The /s/ is deleted and a /ʃ/ is added from the vowel
quests.correctAnswer: The /s/ and /j/ blend into /ʃ/, as the tongue moves back for the /j/
quests.hint: Say “this year” slowly, then quickly. Notice where your tongue goes after the hiss.
quests.explanation: The tongue is shaped for /s/ at the front of the mouth and must move to the palatal position for /j/. Instead of making two separate movements, speakers blend them into /ʃ/: “thi-shear”. The spelling plays no part; the sounds do. Time words like “this year” are good practice.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescence is driven by articulation: the tongue blade moves toward the palate for /j/, so /s/ shifts to /ʃ/ and the two sounds fuse.

quests.instruction: Apply the pattern to “press your” in “Press your thumb here”. Which spoken form fits?
options: “press-your”: both sounds are pronounced separately
“pre-zhyer”: they blend into /ʒ/
“pre-shyer”: the /s/ and /j/ blend into /ʃ/ before a weak “your”
“pre-chyer”: they blend into /tʃ/
quests.correctAnswer: “pre-shyer”: the /s/ and /j/ blend into /ʃ/ before a weak “your”
quests.hint: Check the last sound of “press” and decide which of the four blends it joins.
quests.explanation: “Press” ends in /s/ and “your” begins with /j/, so the blend is /ʃ/: “pre-shyer”. “Your” is weak here (/jə/), which makes the blend even more natural. Instructions and notices are full of this pattern.
quests.phoneticRule: Weak “your” (/jə/) is a typical trigger for coalescence, because its initial /j/ is brief and unstressed.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “as usual” fits “Late again, as usual”?
options: “uh-zyoo-zhoo-ul”: the /z/ stays and is followed by a clear /j/ glide
“uh-joo-zhoo-ul”: the /z/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/
“uh-zhoo-zhoo-ul”: the /z/ and /j/ blend into /ʒ/, as in “vision”
“uh-shoo-zhoo-ul”: the /z/ and /j/ blend into /ʃ/
quests.correctAnswer: “uh-zhoo-zhoo-ul”: the /z/ and /j/ blend into /ʒ/, as in “vision”
quests.hint: The first word ends in a voiced /z/. Pick the blend that is also voiced.
quests.explanation: “As” ends in /z/ and “usual” begins with /j/, so the pair blends into /ʒ/, the sound in the middle of “vision”: “uh-zhoo-zhoo-ul”. The word “usual” already contains /ʒ/ in the middle, so the phrase has two of the same sound. Hearing both helps you identify it quickly.
quests.phoneticRule: Voiced /z/ + /j/ gives voiced /ʒ/, parallel to /s/ + /j/ giving /ʃ/.

quests.instruction: Which sound is heard at the start of “your” in “How’s your sister?”
options: A /ʒ/ blend, as in “vision”: “how-zhyer”
A /dʒ/ blend, as in “jam”: “how-jyer”
A /ʃ/ blend, as in “shoe”: “how-shyer”
A clear /j/ only, with the /z/ dropped
quests.correctAnswer: A /ʒ/ blend, as in “vision”: “how-zhyer”
quests.hint: The /z/ in “how’s” is voiced, so choose the result that keeps that buzz.
quests.explanation: “How’s” ends in /z/, and “your” begins with /j/, so the result is /ʒ/: “how-zhyer”. Everyday questions about people use this blend all the time. A blend with /ʃ/ would lose the voicing, and /dʒ/ would add a stop.
quests.phoneticRule: The blend of /z/ and /j/ keeps voicing and fricative quality, so it is /ʒ/ rather than the affricate /dʒ/.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Who’s your teacher?”
options: “whoz-your”: both words are pronounced separately
“who-jyer”: they blend into /dʒ/
“who-syer”: the /z/ loses its voice and stays separate
“who-zhyer”: the /z/ and weak “your” blend into /ʒ/
quests.correctAnswer: “who-zhyer”: the /z/ and weak “your” blend into /ʒ/
quests.hint: Predict the blend from the sounds before you read the options: a voiced /z/ meets /j/.
quests.explanation: “Who’s” ends in /z/, and “your” begins with /j/. They blend into /ʒ/: “who-zhyer”. The same result appears in “is your”, “does your” and “has your”, so you can predict it with any /z/ + /j/.
quests.phoneticRule: The blend applies to the /z/ of contractions and auxiliaries as well as to the /z/ of full words.

quests.instruction: What sound results where “bad” and “you” meet in “Too bad you missed it”?
options: /tʃ/, as in “chip”: the voiced stop becomes voiceless
/dʒ/, as in “jump”: the voiced stop becomes a voiced affricate
/ʃ/, as in “ship”: the stop turns into a fricative
/ʒ/, as in “vision”: the stop turns into a voiced fricative sound
quests.correctAnswer: /dʒ/, as in “jump”: the voiced stop becomes a voiced affricate
quests.hint: Check whether the first sound is a stop or a fricative, and whether it is voiced.
quests.explanation: “Bad” ends in the voiced stop /d/. A voiced stop + /j/ gives the voiced affricate /dʒ/. If the first sound were voiceless, you would get /tʃ/; if it were a fricative, you would get /ʃ/ or /ʒ/. So two questions decide the result: stop or fricative, voiced or voiceless.
quests.phoneticRule: Predict the blend with two features: manner (stop gives affricate, fricative gives fricative) and voicing (kept from the first sound).

quests.instruction: Compare “this year” and “his year”. Why does one give /ʃ/ and the other /ʒ/?
options: “his” is stressed in this phrase, so the stress changes the blend into a voiced sound
/ʒ/ is used only after an unstressed word
The vowel of “year” decides the voicing
The first sound keeps its voicing: voiceless /s/ gives /ʃ/, voiced /z/ gives /ʒ/
quests.correctAnswer: The first sound keeps its voicing: voiceless /s/ gives /ʃ/, voiced /z/ gives /ʒ/
quests.hint: Compare the last sound of “this” with the last sound of “his”. What differs between them?
quests.explanation: “This” ends in voiceless /s/ and “his” ends in voiced /z/. The blend copies the voicing of the first sound: /ʃ/ is voiceless and /ʒ/ is voiced. Stress and the following vowel do not decide it. So hearing a buzzing “zh” tells you the first sound was /z/.
quests.phoneticRule: Voicing is preserved across coalescence: voiceless inputs give /tʃ/ or /ʃ/, and voiced inputs give /dʒ/ or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: Which result fits “Bet you can’t guess”?
options: /tʃ/: “be-choo”
/dʒ/: “be-joo”
/ʃ/: “be-shoo”
/ʒ/: “be-zhoo”
quests.correctAnswer: /tʃ/: “be-choo”
quests.hint: Use the test from the first question on the word “bet”: decide its manner and its voicing, then pick the matching blend.
quests.explanation: “Bet” ends in /t/, a voiceless stop, so the blend is the voiceless affricate /tʃ/: “be-choo”. Using the two-feature test lets you work out any blend, even in a phrase you have not met.
quests.phoneticRule: The two-feature test (manner and voicing) predicts the blend for any of the four cases: /t/ gives /tʃ/, /d/ gives /dʒ/, /s/ gives /ʃ/, /z/ gives /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: In “When did you arrive?”, which spoken form of “did you” is typical?
options: “did-you”: both words are strong with a clear /j/ and a pause
“di-ya”: the /d/ is dropped, so the blend does not occur
“di-ja”, with a /dʒ/ blend, followed by the vowel of “arrive”
“di-cha arrive”: the /d/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/ before “arrive”
quests.correctAnswer: “di-ja”, with a /dʒ/ blend, followed by the vowel of “arrive”
quests.hint: Say the question as a friend would, at normal speed, and listen to the sound where “did” ends.
quests.explanation: Questions with “did you” are among the most common sentences in English, and the blend happens in the middle of the question: “When di-ja arrive?”. A listener who expects “did you” as two clear words may not recognise it. So hearing /dʒ/ here should trigger the thought “did you”.
quests.phoneticRule: In wh-questions, the auxiliary and “you” are both unstressed, which makes the blend /d/ + /j/ → /dʒ/ especially frequent.

quests.instruction: Why does “would you” in “Which would you prefer?” sound like “wou-ja”?
options: The word “would” is replaced by “wood” in fast speech
The /d/ meets the weak “you” (/jə/), and the two blend into /dʒ/
The /j/ moves back onto “would”, so that “would” gains a /j/ at its end
Question words trigger a /dʒ/ sound before “you”
quests.correctAnswer: The /d/ meets the weak “you” (/jə/), and the two blend into /dʒ/
quests.hint: Ignore the question word and look at the two sounds that touch: the end of “would” and the start of “you”.
quests.explanation: The blend depends on the sounds that touch, not on the question word. “Would” ends in /d/ and “you” begins with /j/, so you get /dʒ/: “wou-ja”. The same would happen in a statement. Weak “you” helps because /jə/ is short and quick.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescence is triggered by the adjacent sounds, not by sentence type, so it occurs in statements and questions alike.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “Haven’t you” fits “Haven’t you heard?”
options: “havnt-you”: both are pronounced separately
“havn-chew”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
“havn-jew”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/
“hav-you”: the /n/ and /t/ are both dropped
quests.correctAnswer: “havn-chew”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
quests.hint: Find the last sound of “haven’t” and the first sound of “you”, and recall the result for that pair.
quests.explanation: “Haven’t” ends in /t/ and “you” begins with /j/, so the blend is /tʃ/: “havn-chew”. Negative questions that express surprise (“Haven’t you heard?”) use this blend very often. If you only listened for “have not”, you might miss the question.
quests.phoneticRule: Negative yes/no questions regularly show the /t/ + /j/ blend, because the negative contraction is directly followed by “you”.

quests.instruction: What kind of change is “dohn-choo” in “Don’t you worry”: elision, assimilation, or coalescence?
options: Coalescence: the /t/ and /j/ merge into the new sound /tʃ/
Elision: the /t/ is simply left out
Assimilation: the /t/ takes the place of the /j/ but stays a /t/
Linking: the /t/ moves onto “you” unchanged
quests.correctAnswer: Coalescence: the /t/ and /j/ merge into the new sound /tʃ/
quests.hint: Ask whether both original sounds can still be heard in the result, or whether a third sound has replaced them.
quests.explanation: In “Don’t you”, neither /t/ nor /j/ survives as itself. Both are replaced by /tʃ/, a new sound made from their features. That is coalescence, not elision (a sound lost), assimilation (one sound adapting but still present) or linking (a sound moved unchanged).
quests.phoneticRule: To classify a change, compare input and output: lost sound (elision), same sound altered (assimilation), two sounds replaced by one new sound (coalescence), or unchanged sound moved (linking).

quests.instruction: Why does “bet you” blend, while “bet me” does not blend, in “Bet me a pound”?
options: “me” is a shorter word, so it cannot blend
“me” is stressed, so it blocks all connected-speech changes
Blending happens only before the word “you”, not before any other word at all, such as “me”
Coalescence needs a /j/ beside the /t/; “me” starts with /m/, so only assimilation can occur
quests.correctAnswer: Coalescence needs a /j/ beside the /t/; “me” starts with /m/, so only assimilation can occur
quests.hint: Compare the first sound of “you” with the first sound of “me”, and recall which sounds blend.
quests.explanation: Coalescence is triggered by a /j/, which is the first sound of “you”, “your”, “year” and “usual”. “Me” begins with /m/, so the /t/ can only assimilate to a lip sound: “bep me”. The blend is therefore specific to /j/, not to any following word.
quests.phoneticRule: The trigger for the four blends is a following /j/; other consonants lead to assimilation or elision instead.

quests.instruction: In “Must you go so soon?”, the /t/ is not omitted. Which statement is accurate?
options: Elision: the /t/ is omitted because it follows /s/, as in “mus’ be” and similar phrases
Assimilation: the /t/ moves to the lips
Coalescence: before /j/ the /t/ blends into /tʃ/ instead of being omitted
No change is possible because the /t/ follows /s/
quests.correctAnswer: Coalescence: before /j/ the /t/ blends into /tʃ/ instead of being omitted
quests.hint: Compare “must be” and “must you”. What differs about the sound after the /t/?
quests.explanation: In “must be”, the /t/ is between /s/ and a consonant and is often omitted. In “must you”, the following sound is /j/, which triggers the blend: /tʃ/, as in “mus-chew”. So the same word can show elision or coalescence, depending on what follows.
quests.phoneticRule: The following sound decides the outcome for a word-final /t/: a /j/ triggers coalescence, while other consonants allow elision or assimilation.

quests.instruction: Which two processes make “would you” sound like “wou-ja” in “Pete, would you mind waiting?”
options: Elision of the /d/ and a strong “you”
Assimilation of the /d/ to /j/, plus linking of “you” onto the next word
Only linking: every sound is kept in place
Coalescence of /d/ + /j/ into /dʒ/, and a weak /jə/ for “you”
quests.correctAnswer: Coalescence of /d/ + /j/ into /dʒ/, and a weak /jə/ for “you”
quests.hint: Think about what happens to the /d/ and /j/, and then about how strong the word “you” is.
quests.explanation: Two things occur together: the /d/ and /j/ coalesce into /dʒ/, and “you” is reduced to the weak form /jə/. The weak /jə/ is what makes the blend so easy: a short, unstressed /j/ is readily absorbed. So “wou-ja” is a blend plus a weak form, not just one change.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescence and weak-form reduction reinforce each other: the weaker the “you”, the more likely the blend.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “is your” fits “Tom, is your car ready?”
options: “i-zhuh”: /z/ and a weak /jə/ blend into /ʒ/ plus a weak vowel
“iz-your”: both words are strong and separate
“i-juh”: the blend is /dʒ/ plus a weak vowel
“i-shuh”: the blend is /ʃ/ plus a weak vowel
quests.correctAnswer: “i-zhuh”: /z/ and a weak /jə/ blend into /ʒ/ plus a weak vowel
quests.hint: The first word ends in /z/ and the second is weak. Combine the blend rule with the weak-form rule.
quests.explanation: “Is” ends in /z/ and weak “your” begins with /j/, so you hear /ʒ/ followed by a weak vowel: “i-zhuh”. A strong “your” (/jɔː/) would also blend, but the weak form is the usual one in this question. Both rules from earlier levels operate together.
quests.phoneticRule: The weak form of “your” is /jə/, and its /j/ blends with a preceding /z/ to give /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: Which blends are heard in “Lena, bet you forgot your keys”?
quests.word: Lena, bet you forgot your keys
quests.textToSpeak: Lena, bet you forgot your keys
options: /dʒ/ in “bet you” and /tʃ/ in “forgot your”
/tʃ/ in “bet you” and /tʃ/ in “forgot your”
/ʃ/ in “bet you” and /ʒ/ in “forgot your”
Only “bet you” blends; “forgot your” keeps a clear /j/
quests.correctAnswer: /tʃ/ in “bet you” and /tʃ/ in “forgot your”
quests.hint: Find the last sound of each word before “you” or “your”, and apply the same rule twice.
quests.explanation: Both “bet” and “forgot” end in /t/, and both are followed by a /j/ word. Each junction blends into /tʃ/: “be-choo for-got-chyer”. One sentence can thus contain several blends, so it helps to listen for the “ch” sounds.
quests.phoneticRule: The blend rule applies at every qualifying junction in a sentence, so repeated /t/ + /j/ pairs give repeated /tʃ/ sounds.

quests.instruction: In a noisy room you hear “Can-cha see it from here?” Which sentence was most likely said?
quests.word: Can’t you see it from here
quests.textToSpeak: Can’t you see it from here
options: “Can you see it from here?”
“Cat you see it from here?”
“Can’t you see it from here?”
“Can’t she see it from here?”
quests.correctAnswer: “Can’t you see it from here?”
quests.hint: Listen for the “ch” sound. Which phrase would give /tʃ/ at the boundary?
quests.explanation: The “ch” sound before a weak vowel could come from /t/ + /j/ in “can’t you”. “Can you” would not give /tʃ/, since there is no /t/. “Cat you” is not a natural sentence. So the blend itself is the clue that the speaker said “can’t”.
quests.phoneticRule: A /tʃ/ at a word boundary before a weak vowel is a cue that the first word ended in /t/, which can distinguish “can’t you” from “can you”.

quests.instruction: You hear “Sara, cou-ja wait here?” Which sentence was most likely said?
options: “Sara, could you wait here?”
“Sara, good you wait here?”
“Sara, could she wait here?”
“Sara, couldn’t you wait here?”
quests.correctAnswer: “Sara, could you wait here?”
quests.hint: Match the /dʒ/ sound with a word that ends in /d/ and the weak “you”.
quests.explanation: “Cou-ja” fits “could you”, with /d/ + /j/ → /dʒ/. “Good you” would also give /dʒ/ but does not make a natural request. “Could she” has no /j/, and “couldn’t you” would have a /t/ and give /tʃ/. Context and sound together point to “could you”.
quests.phoneticRule: A /dʒ/ blend signals a preceding /d/, and the choice among candidates is settled by grammar and context.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “does your” fits “Ruth, does your mum know?”
options: “duz-your”: both words are strong and separate, with a clear /j/ in “your”
“duh-juh”: they blend into /dʒ/
“duh-shuh”: they blend into /ʃ/
“duh-zhuh”: the /z/ and a weak “your” blend into /ʒ/
quests.correctAnswer: “duh-zhuh”: the /z/ and a weak “your” blend into /ʒ/
quests.hint: The buzzing /z/ meets /j/. Which blend keeps the buzz and is a smooth fricative?
quests.explanation: “Does” ends in voiced /z/, so the blend with /j/ is voiced /ʒ/, followed by a weak vowel: “duh-zhuh”. Putting this stage together: stops give /tʃ/ or /dʒ/, fricatives give /ʃ/ or /ʒ/, and voicing is copied from the first sound.
quests.phoneticRule: The four blends form a system: manner (stop or fricative) and voicing of the first sound determine the result when /j/ follows.
